body: Hou, Xue and Zhang (Review of Financial Studies 33(5), 2020; NBER w23394; ~890 Semantic Scholar citations) rebuilt 452 published US cross-sectional anomalies (1967-2014) using NYSE breakpoints and value-weighted returns, so that tiny illiquid stocks cannot drive the result. 65% (about 296) failed the ordinary |t| >= 1.96 hurdle; with the multiple-testing hurdle of t >= 2.78 the failure rate rose to 82%. Trading-friction anomalies (short-term reversal, idiosyncratic volatility, liquidity, max return) were the weakest; 96% failed. What survived were mostly value-versus-growth, profitability, investment (asset growth) and momentum effects, and even those shrink once their q-factor model is applied. Replicated? The paper is itself the replication, but it is disputed: Chen-Zimmermann and Jensen-Kelly-Pedersen argue the failures come mainly from value-weighting, which mutes effects that live in small firms. Use for us: when we read a screen or newsletter citing 'an academic anomaly', ask whether it holds in value-weighted, non-microcap tests. Our Indian small-cap universe is exactly where anomalies look strongest and are hardest to trade (impact cost, circuit limits), so haircut any paper result before relying on it.
title: Hou-Xue-Zhang 'Replicating Anomalies' (RFS 2020): most of 452 published anomalies fail once microcaps are tamed
